builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: AgenTest: Mining Business Rules to Test LLM Agents for Business Logic Bugs
summary: AgenTest replaces manual business-rule test writing and success-only or policy-based agent evaluation with automatic mining of system prompts, tool definitions, and domain knowledge into Given-When-Then specifications, each exercised via multi-turn interactions and a hybrid oracle over messages, tool calls, and state. The cost is the engineering to build satisfying environment states and simulated users per specification, plus LLM and orchestration expense for multi-turn test execution; the paper shows no turnkey tool, so adoption means reimplementing the pipeline. It can fail where rules remain implicit and unmined, where environment instantiation is infeasible for real production systems, or where the hybrid oracle misjudges ambiguous traces, producing false positives or missed violations.
rationale: The approach directly addresses production business-logic risk in tool-using agents with commodity infrastructure, but its value depends on validating that mined rules and oracles transfer to the reader's own domain. About 60% of bug-triggering runs being invisible from final state alone supports adopting trajectory-level checking regardless of this specific system.
technique: Mining business rules into executable agent test specifications

claims.statement: AgenTest replaces manual business-rule test writing and success-only or policy-based agent evaluation with automatic mining of system prompts, tool definitions, and domain knowledge into Given-When-Then specifications, each exercised via multi-turn interactions and a hybrid oracle over messages, tool calls, and state. The cost is the engineering to build satisfying environment states and simulated users per specification, plus LLM and orchestration expense for multi-turn test execution; the paper shows no turnkey tool, so adoption means reimplementing the pipeline. It can fail where rules remain implicit and unmined, where environment instantiation is infeasible for real production systems, or where the hybrid oracle misjudges ambiguous traces, producing false positives or missed violations.
On tau2-bench agents, detects violations of 89 and 121 distinct business-rule specifications, 3.4x and 2.5x as many as all baselines combined, including cross-user data access bugs missed otherwise.
